title: You Are a God Who Sees — Servant, Flight, Well
blocks: Brothers and sisters, the last lesson ended under a sky full of stars: Abram believed Yahweh, and Yahweh credited it to him for righteousness. And then God walked that path of blood alone, and the covenant was cut.
And then Genesis 16:1 says, "Now Sarai, Abram's wife, bore him no children."

The summit of chapter 15 is followed straight away by the wreckage of chapter 16. And the question this lesson puts to us is an intensely practical one: the decisions that do us the most damage are usually not the ones we make when we are angry. They are the ones we make when we cannot bear to wait any longer. When a person is angry, he at least knows he is angry. When a person can no longer stand the waiting, he thinks he is only "working something out".

Let me put the answer at the front. When we cannot wait any longer, we start working things out for ourselves. And in the wreckage those solutions leave behind, the first person God goes looking for is the one nobody sees.
Verse 3 carries a small note about time: "after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan."

Brothers and sisters, do the arithmetic with me. Genesis 12:4 says he was seventy-five years old when he left Haran, so by now he is eighty-five. From the day God said, "I will make of you a great nation," to this moment, ten years have gone by.

How many times in those ten years had God spoken the promise? Chapter 12 said a great nation. Chapter 13 said offspring like the dust of the earth. Chapter 15 said offspring like the stars of the sky — and the covenant had only just been cut.
Ten years. Four promises. Not one child.

I want you to stop here for a moment, because if we rush straight on to blaming her we will learn nothing at all from this chapter. Sarai was not a frivolous woman. She waited ten years. And in that culture, the shame carried by a woman who bore no children is something we today can barely imagine.

The first thing she says in verse 2 is theologically flawless: "Yahweh has restrained me from bearing." The Hebrew is עֲצָרַנִי יְהוָה (*atsarani YHWH*) — Yahweh has held me back. She believes God is sovereign, and she believes this matter is in God's hands.
The trouble is in the second half of the sentence: "Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her."

Brothers and sisters, here is the deepest lesson in the chapter: she acknowledges God's sovereignty without ever handing that sovereignty over. Her theology is correct — but she took that correct sentence as grounds for closing the case rather than as grounds for waiting.

And "I will obtain children by her" is, in the original, אִבָּנֶה מִמֶּנָּה (*ibaneh mimenah*), literally "I shall be built up from her." The word for "build", בנה, and the word for "son", בֵּן, come from the same root. In that world, to have a son was to be built up — so she is not merely asking for a child. She is asking to be put back on her feet.
Sarai giving her servant to her husband was a perfectly legal arrangement in that day. So why is it still wrong?

Legal documents of the period — the Nuzi tablets and the Code of Hammurabi, for instance — do contain arrangements of exactly this kind, so what they did was in line with the rules of their time. But this chapter is putting a different question to us: legal is not the same as in line with God's heart. God had said plainly in chapter 15, "he who will come out of your own body will be your heir", and they took a method everybody else was using and finished God's promise for him with it. This is intensely practical for us. A great many wrong turns do not begin with a bad motive at all. They begin with "everyone does it this way" and "this way is faster". So when you weigh a course of action, it is not enough to ask whether it is legal, or whether it is the done thing. There is one more question to ask: is this the road God actually named?
Ten years of waiting — why does God make people wait so long?

The text gives no reason, and we should not invent one on God's behalf. But one fact is visible: those ten years accomplished something — little by little they wore away every remaining possibility that this could still be managed by human strength. By chapter 17 Abraham is ninety-nine, Sarah's childbearing years are long past, and a child born then is a child the whole world can see was not produced by anyone's effort. So waiting is very often not delay. It is the clearing of the field. And the reminder for us is this: while you are waiting, alongside the question "when?", you can also ask, "which crutch are you taking away from me?" And let us say it honestly as well: not every season of waiting is one we can understand. Some we understand only much later, and some we never understand in this life.
2. A Light from the Original: This Is Chapter 3 All Over Again
From the second half of verse 2 into verse 3, the author uses a very deliberate set of verbs. I want to read them to you one at a time.

"Abram listened to the voice of Sarai" — וַיִּשְׁמַע לְקוֹל (*vayishma leqol*), "listened to the voice of". Brothers and sisters, in Genesis 3:17 God says to Adam, "Because you have listened to your wife's voice", and it is the identical phrase.

"Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant … and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife" — "took", וַתִּקַּח; "gave", וַתִּתֵּן. And Genesis 3:6 says of Eve, "she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her" — the same pair of verbs, in the same order: she takes, she gives, and he eats, he listens.
Even the word for "her husband", אִישָׁהּ, is the same word that stands in Genesis 3:6.

Brothers and sisters, the author never has to write the sentence "this was wrong." He has only to use the vocabulary of chapter 3, and the reader understands. This is the same thing happening a second time: not waiting for God to speak, but reaching out and taking.

And notice that there are two people here who bear responsibility. Sarai proposes it; Abram "listened". From the first verse of this chapter to the last, Abram never once enquires of God — the man who had just cut a covenant with God under the stars does not, this time, so much as ask.

And the consequences arrive at once. Verse 4: "When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes." The root behind "despised", וַתֵּקַל (*vateqal*), is "light" — in Hagar's eyes, her mistress had become light. Brothers and sisters, that word is the exact opposite of "glory", כָּבֵד, which means heavy.

In verse 5 Sarai says to Abram, "This wrong is your fault." The word behind "wrong" is חֲמָסִי (*chamasi*), from the root חָמָס — an extremely heavy word. Genesis 6:11 says "the earth was filled with violence", and this is the very word it uses. She reaches for the vocabulary of the flood chapter to describe what she is suffering inside her own household.
In verse 6 Abram says, "Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes." And then: "Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face."

Brothers and sisters, "dealt harshly with her" in this verse is וַתְּעַנֶּהָ (*vate'aneha*), and it is the same word used in Exodus 1:11–12 when the Egyptians afflict the Israelites. An Egyptian slave-girl is dealt with harshly inside a Hebrew tent, and the verb is precisely the verb that will later describe Israel's affliction in Egypt. The author is laying down a very deep marker here.
Three people, three wounds: Sarai is made light of, Hagar is dealt with harshly, and Abram will not risk offending either side. And every bit of it began with one decision to "work something out".
"Her mistress was despised in her eyes" — why does the text bother to record that line?

Because it lets us see that nobody in this story comes out clean. Sarai proposes it, Abram goes along with it, Hagar conceives and makes light of her mistress, Sarai deals harshly with her, Hagar runs. The text does not prettify a single one of them. In verse 5 Sarai says, "This wrong is your fault", pushing the responsibility onto her husband; in verse 6 Abram says, "Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes", which amounts to washing his hands of the whole thing. A household disaster was brought about by three people together. And the reminder for us is this: when something goes wrong at home, the least useful thing anyone can do is work out who is most to blame; the most useful thing is that each person looks first at his own share.
The manuscript says this is chapter 3 all over again. How is a correspondence like that actually spotted?

Watch the verbs. In chapter 3 the woman "took" the fruit, "gave" it to her husband, and the husband "listened" to his wife's voice. In chapter 16 Sarai "took" her servant, "gave" her to her husband, and Abram "listened" to the voice of Sarai. Three verbs, in the same order. Hebrew narrative loves to pass comment this way — it does not say outright "this was wrong"; it lets you recognise the sentence pattern for yourself. That is excellent training for reading Scripture: watch for repeated verbs and repeated sentence shapes, because that is very often where the author is delivering his verdict. And what this particular echo is telling us is that this was no simple domestic arrangement. It is the same old complaint: taking God's promise into our own hands and finishing it ourselves.
3. God Goes First to the One Who Was Thrown Away
Verse 7: "Yahweh's angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur."
Brothers and sisters, stop here, and think about how extraordinary that is.
Who made this wreckage? Sarai proposed it and Abram agreed to it. So by our logic, God ought to go and have a word with Abram first, or begin by rebuking Sarai.
But the one God goes to first is the runaway Egyptian slave-girl.

And this is the first appearance of "Yahweh's angel" in the Bible. The first time in all of Scripture that this messenger is recorded as appearing to anybody, it is not inside Abraham's tent, and it is not beside an altar. It is by a spring of water out in the wilderness, and the person he appears to stands at the very bottom of that society — a foreign slave-girl, just driven out by her mistress, pregnant, with nowhere on earth to go.
Brothers and sisters, that is the kind of person God comes in person to find first. That fact, all by itself, is the gospel.
And the first thing he says to her is this: "Hagar, Sarai's servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?"

Notice two things. First, he calls her by her name. In the whole chapter Sarai never once uses her name — in verse 5 and again in verse 6 Sarai calls her only "my servant" and "your maid". Abram never uses it either. The first one in the entire chapter to call her by name is God.

Second, what he asks is "Where did you come from? Where are you going?" That is the same kind of question as "Where are you?" in Genesis 3:9 — God is not short of information; he wants the person to say it out loud herself.

And Hagar's answer is very honest: "I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai." She answers the first half of the question and leaves the second half unanswered. Because there was nowhere at all for her to go.
Why does God go to Hagar first, rather than dealing with the problem in Abram's household?

Because God always goes first to the one who has been thrown away. Hagar is a foreigner, a slave-woman, the one who was used and then dealt with harshly — the person with the least voice in that whole society. And the first time in all of Scripture that "Yahweh's angel" appears to a human being, he appears to her. That carries a strong correction for the church: our own order of business is usually to take care of the people with influence first, and God's order is usually the reverse. In practice it works out like this: when something goes wrong in a family or a team, go first to the person with the least say, the one most easily sacrificed, and ask how he is doing. That is not merely compassion. That is doing things the way God does them.
4. You Are a God Who Sees
Verse 9 is the verse in this chapter that has to be handled with the greatest care: "Yahweh's angel said to her, 'Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.'"
Brothers and sisters, I want to say the next few sentences with great deliberateness, because this verse has been misused, and the cost of that misuse is that somebody goes on suffering.

First, look at the order of the context. What does God say on either side of telling her to go back? Verse 10: "I will greatly multiply your offspring, that they will not be counted for multitude." Verse 11: "Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction."

That is to say, God does not send her back empty-handed. He first gives her a promise larger than anything Sarai holds — "greatly multiply your offspring", a sentence that until now had been spoken to Abraham. She goes back carrying an identity, not carrying fear.

Second, look at the situation she was in. A pregnant woman alone in the wilderness is not a free woman; she is on a road that ends in death. When God tells her to go back, he is telling her to stay alive.

Third — and this is the sentence I mean to say most heavily of all: this is a particular instruction for a particular situation, and it is not a universal principle. God never tells anyone to stay in a place where she will be beaten to death, and wait for it there. If someone in your congregation is living inside domestic violence, and you quote this verse to tell her to submit, you have made yourself an accomplice. Get her safe first, and talk about everything else afterwards. When God found Hagar in the wilderness, the first things he gave her were a spring of water and her own name — not a lecture.
And verse 13 is the summit of the whole chapter: "She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, 'You are a God who sees.'"
The Hebrew is אֵל רֳאִי (*El Roi*) — "the God who sees me".

Brothers and sisters, do you realise how astonishing that is? In the whole Bible, the first human being ever to give God a name is a slave-woman out of Egypt. Earlier than Abraham. Earlier than Moses.

She goes on to say, "Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?" A woman who had spent her whole life being treated as an instrument, as a problem, as one piece on somebody else's board, discovers for the first time that there is One who genuinely sees her.

And from that day the well had a name: Beer Lahai Roi, which means "the well of the Living One who sees me". Brothers and sisters, remember this well, because Genesis 24:62 tells us that Isaac later lived beside it. God did not forget the place where a discarded woman met him.
The angel tells Hagar to "return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands". Is that telling a person to go back and endure being bullied?

This verse has to be spoken clearly; there is no room here for vagueness. First, the situation in the text is this: she is pregnant, alone in the wilderness, on the road towards Egypt, and for a solitary pregnant woman that road is lethal. And before the angel tells her to go back, he first gives her an enormous promise — "I will greatly multiply your offspring." In other words, going back is a going back with a guarantee, not a going back empty-handed. Second, and this is what matters most: this verse may never be used to tell anybody to remain in a violent, abusive or dangerous relationship. Scripture says plainly elsewhere that the oppressed are to be protected. If you, or someone you know, is being harmed, please seek safe help and professional resources immediately — that is the biblical course of action.
"You are a God who sees" — what is special about that sentence in the original?

The name Hagar gives to God is אֵל רֳאִי (*El Roi*), which means "the God who sees me". It is the only time in the whole Bible that a human being gives God a name, and the one who does it is a foreign slave-woman. And the well that follows is called Beer Lahai Roi — "the well of the Living One who sees me". So the heart of this passage is not that her problem was solved. It is that she was seen. For a great many people that is the very sentence they most need to hear: you think nobody knows you have been crying, and there is One who knows. Notice too that the first words God speaks to her are her own name — "Hagar, Sarai's servant." He knows who she is, and he knows where she has come from.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is putting the whole responsibility onto Sarai. Verse 2 says plainly, "Abram listened to the voice of Sarai", and that phrase is identical to the one in Genesis 3:17. What is more, Abram never once enquires of God in this entire chapter, and when the thing blows up he says, "Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes" — he pushes the woman back and steps aside himself. If you rebuke only Sarai, the sisters sitting in front of you will go home with the impression that once again it was a woman who caused the trouble, and that is not what the text says.

The second is preaching "return to your mistress" as God permitting oppression. We have already dealt with that. This verse has to be preached together with the promises of verses 10 and 11, and you must say it out loud: this is not a universal principle requiring victims to endure.

The third is preaching Hagar as the chief culprit. She was handed over; she had no say in it at all. The attitude of the text towards her is compassion from beginning to end, not blame. If you preach her as the woman who ruined everything, your congregation will never learn the heart of a God who sees people.

The fourth is using Ishmael's descendants to argue that some modern people group lies under a curse. In verse 10 God promises to multiply her offspring greatly; Genesis 21:20 says, "God was with the boy, and he grew"; Genesis 17:20 says God will make him fruitful and multiply him exceedingly. To read this as a curse is to preach God's mercy backwards. And to use it as an explanation of today's international conflicts is to turn Scripture into news commentary.

The fifth is preaching verse 12, "He will be like a wild donkey among men", as an insult. Job 39:5–8 uses the wild donkey to picture a creature nobody has broken to harness, living free out in the wilderness. That is the description of a way of life, not a moral verdict. And in the context of this verse it even carries a kind of blessing for the son of a slave-woman — his descendants will not be slaves.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese families have traditionally carried the weight of the old saying that of the three unfilial acts, leaving no descendant is the worst — and in the past there really were the practices of taking a concubine and of obtaining a child through another woman's body. What does this chapter say about that? Brothers and sisters, the answer this chapter gives is very clear, and it does not give it by moralising. It gives it through consequences. Sarai's method was legal in her day — marriage contracts in the ancient Near East really did carry clauses providing for a servant to bear the child where the wife was childless. But the outcome Scripture records is this: the mistress is made light of, the servant is dealt with harshly, the husband comes out badly with both women, and the crack in this household keeps widening all the way into chapter 21, where it ends with a woman being sent off into the wilderness with her child. And in the whole book of Genesis, not one household with more than one wife is a household at peace. So mark the distinction carefully: that Scripture records something does not mean Scripture approves it. And the way to tell is very simple — when you have finished reading, do you want a family like that? As for couples living today under the pressure to conceive, let me say something pastoral. God does not rebuke Sarai in this chapter for wanting a child. What he rebukes is never the longing. It is the move that says, "I will work something out." You may ask, you may weep, you may ask again year after year; what you may not do is settle the timing on God's behalf.

The second question: I have domestic help at home, or people working under me, or a foreign carer — how do I treat them in a way that fits Scripture? Brothers and sisters, this chapter hands us an extremely sharp test. In the whole chapter Sarai speaks of Hagar three times and never once uses her name; she says only "my servant". Abram says, "your maid is in your hand." And God, the moment he opens his mouth, uses her full name: "Hagar, Sarai's servant." A name is the first line of the test. Do you remember the name of the person who works in your house every day? Do you know how many children she has at home? Then there is this line: "Do to her whatever is good in your eyes." That sentence was entirely valid in law — she genuinely was property. But what the text records next is "Sarai dealt harshly with her." Brothers and sisters, the people you have the right to treat however you like are precisely the place where your life is most truthfully exposed. Colossians 4:1 says, "Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven."
7. Living 321 Out — Acknowledge His Sovereignty, and Hand It Over Too
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — God goes first to the one who was thrown away. And in Luke 15 the Lord Jesus tells of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost. In John 4 he sits waiting at a well at noon for a Samaritan woman. Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: his feet always move towards the margin first. So a church that is genuinely learning from him will ask "who is not here?" before it asks "how many came today?"

The Bible is my standard — this chapter shows us something very sobering: what Sarai said was theologically correct. "Yahweh has restrained me from bearing" — entirely correct. And yet correct theology, once it is taken up as the reason for an action, can still produce a disaster. So having a standard is not merely knowing the right doctrine. It is letting the right doctrine run the whole course — including the stretch that says, "and therefore I will wait."

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice what is missing from this chapter. From verse 1 to verse 6, not one person prays. In that whole stretch there is not a single line saying they enquired of Yahweh. Brothers and sisters, a great deal of wreckage comes about not because we did not know, but because we did not ask. And then in verse 7, God comes himself — he did not wait to be asked.

Let Jesus be King — Sarai acknowledged God's sovereignty, and never handed that sovereignty over. Those two things stand a long way apart. To acknowledge sovereignty is to say, "this matter is in God's hands." To hand sovereignty over is to say, "and therefore the timing is in his hands too." Brothers and sisters, it is on that second half that we most often trip. We agree that God is sovereign; we simply disagree with his schedule.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — in this chapter not one human being does the right thing, and the only figure who gives off any light is the God who goes looking for someone out in the wilderness. So this chapter must not be preached as a lesson in morals. It has to be preached as an appearing: after people have wrecked the thing, God walks into the wreckage of his own accord.

Establish God's system — that well, Beer Lahai Roi, later became the place where Isaac lived. Brothers and sisters, God remembers the places where discarded people met him, and he settles the next generation there. So to establish God's system is to count in the people who have been overlooked — if your list holds only "useful people", that is not God's system.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about selflessness, and this chapter hands us a very concrete warning. On the surface, Sarai's method looks exactly like denying of self — she gave her own husband over to another woman in order to bring God's promise about. She sacrificed her own place. But that sacrifice was not selflessness. It was a takeover. So remember this: the test of selflessness is not how much you gave up. It is whose hands the sovereignty is in. A person who is very good at sacrificing, but insists on sacrificing in his own way, is still living the self-centred life.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Well
Brothers and sisters, the same well in the wilderness falls into four different hearts, and what each of them sees is not the same.

The proud heart says, "Sarai really had very little faith." What this heart is best at, reading this chapter, is analysing somebody else's failure. Brothers and sisters, take note: Sarai waited ten years. Have you ever waited ten years for anything? Until you have reached your own tenth year of waiting, hold back from assessing her quite so confidently.

The fearful heart says, "Am I working things out for myself too?" Having read this, that heart begins to doubt every decision it makes, until in the end it dares to do nothing at all. To that heart I want to say: the way to tell is not by refusing to act, it is by whether you asked. Sarai's problem was not that she did something. It was that she did not ask before she did it, and she did not turn back after she had done it. You may act — as long as you are asking all the way along.

The ashamed heart says, "I am the one with no name." It may be that at home, at work, or in church, you have always been the one who is ordered about, arranged around, and never asked what you think. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the first person God calls by name in this chapter is exactly that kind of person. And the name she gave God was "the God who sees me". It is not that nobody sees you. It is that the One who sees you was never on your list.

The wounded heart says, "Then what about me? I am the one who was thrown away." It may be that you really were used, really were taken advantage of, and then left at the side. Brothers and sisters, this chapter does not win Hagar any justice — the text records no apology from Sarai, and it records not one word spoken by Abram on her behalf. That is very honest of it. But it does record this: God found her, called her by name, heard her affliction, and gave her a promise. Sometimes what we want is justice, and what God gives first is sight. And that well, in the end, became the place where the next generation lived.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, identify the matter you are currently "working out" for yourself. Write it down, and then write one honest sentence beside it: is this faith, or is this me unable to wait any longer? Nobody else has to see the answer.

Second, say one person's name out loud. This week, take somebody you normally address only by their job — the security guard, the cleaner, the carer, the delivery rider — call them once by name, and then remember it. The first thing God does in this chapter is say a name.

Third, practise enquiring of God once. Take one decision this week, large or small, and before you make it stop and pray for three minutes, and then talk it over with a spiritual companion. The disaster of Sarai and Abram began with a decision nobody ever asked about.

Fourth, pray for one person who is not on the list. Think about your small group and your church: who has been missing for a long time without anyone mentioning him? Pray for him this week, and send him a message.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. There is a slave-woman in the Bible whose mistress used her as an instrument for producing a child, and when she could bear it no longer she fled into the wilderness. The first person God went to find was not the great man who held the promises, but this slave-woman nobody wanted. And she became the first person in the whole Bible to give God a name, and the name she said was: you are the God who sees me.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I acknowledge God's sovereignty, and that I hand that sovereignty over to him; even the timing I leave to him to decide.
I declare that I will no longer dress up "I cannot wait any longer" as "I am working something out for God".
I declare that I will remember the names nobody remembers, because God called those names first.
I declare that I am seen; he is the God who sees me.
This week I am supposed to go and see someone nobody sees, but I am afraid I will do it badly and only make things awkward. What should I do?

Seeing a person takes no technique at all. It only takes stopping. Here are three things with a very low threshold. First, say his name — the first words God speaks to Hagar are her name, and a great many people have gone a very long time in their own surroundings without anyone using theirs. Second, ask one concrete question. Do not ask "how have you been lately?"; ask instead, "what has been the most tiring thing these last few weeks?" Third, when he has finished, do not rush in with advice. Just say, "that really isn't easy." If he does not want to talk, stop there and do not press him. You are not going in order to solve his problem. You are going so that he knows somebody sees him. That much you can certainly do.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be that well out in the wilderness.

A pregnant Egyptian slave-woman, out of the tents and away, walking the road towards Shur — and that road runs down towards Egypt. She is going home. And she must have known well enough what waits in Egypt for a slave who has run away.
And then, beside a spring of water, someone stopped her, and said her name out loud.
Brothers and sisters, in the whole chapter nobody asks her what she wants. Sarai does not ask. Abram does not ask. The first one to ask her "where did you come from? Where are you going?" is God.
And the name she gave God — "the God who sees me" — became one of the tenderest names for God in all of Scripture.

There is one more thing I want you to see. The last verse of this chapter says, "Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram." And Isaac will not be born until Abraham is a hundred. Which is to say, after this chapter God is silent for thirteen years — chapter 17 opens with the words, "When Abram was ninety-nine years old."

Thirteen years. What we get in exchange for working things out ourselves is a very long silence. And yet thirteen years later, when God opens his mouth again, the first thing he says is, "I am God Almighty."
Brothers and sisters, he had not given up. He simply waited until the man had truly run out of methods, and then he spoke his own name.

The focus is not on how long I have waited, not on the methods I once resorted to, and not on whether anyone has seen how badly I was treated. The focus is on Jesus — he is the good shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go after one sheep. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to stop our own methods, and to go and say out loud a name nobody has said. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ "Took, gave, listened" — chapter 16 replays the three verbs of chapter 3. What does that old complaint look like in our own day?
2. ★★★ What they did was legal and conventional in their own time, and the outcome was a disaster. What principle of judgement does that give us?
3. ★ The first time in all of Scripture that anyone gives God a name, it is a foreign slave-woman. What is that saying to us?
4. ★★ The one God goes to first is the one who was thrown away. How should that order correct the habits we bring to handling things?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I will work something out on God's behalf), fearful (if I wait any longer it will be too late), ashamed (I am the one who gets used), wounded (nobody sees what I have given). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "You are a God who sees." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something right now that you have waited on so long you have started thinking of taking it into your own hands? What is the method you were planning to use?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The one thing I most want somebody to see about me is …"
9. ★★ This week, which person that nobody sees will you go and see? Say the name, say the time, and say the one question you will ask.

Leader's reminder: question nine may touch experiences of being used and being sacrificed. If someone speaks about being harmed within their own family, do not adjudicate rights and wrongs inside the group; follow up with him privately after the meeting. If violence or abuse is involved, you must help him find safe help and professional resources, and you must never urge anyone back into danger.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, who is the one most easily taken for granted? What will you do this week to let that person be seen?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who is the person whose name nobody remembers?

12. ★★★ The practice of saying names: this week, deliberately say three people's names out loud, and ask each of them, "what has been the most tiring thing these last few weeks?" Say who you will start with.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and this week tell him your answer to question nine, and ask him to hold you back from taking things into your own hands. Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, the first person in the Bible ever to give God a name was a runaway slave-woman. Second, the name she gave was "you are the God who sees me". Third, so I believe in a God who is certain to see the people nobody else sees. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the person you will go and see this week, and the matter you are waiting on but have begun wanting to take into your own hands. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to give us the faith to keep waiting, and eyes that see people.
